greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gathers us in His love today.
penitential:
Lord Jesus, you are the light that shines in the darkness: Lord, have mercy.
Christ Jesus, you heal the brokenhearted and bind up their wounds: Christ, have mercy.
Lord Jesus, you are the resurrection and the life: Lord, have mercy.
psalm_response: Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord.
homily:
We begin today with an image that is perhaps the most ordinary thing in the world: a ledger. Think of it. A book of accounts. Lines ruled in red ink, columns for what is owed, columns for what has been paid, a bottom line that tells us exactly where we stand. We live our lives by ledgers, don't we? We track our time, our energy, our resources, our successes, and our failures. We are always calculating. We want to know if we are doing enough, if we are being enough, if the balance of our lives is leaning toward the positive or the negative. In today’s Gospel, Jesus tells us a story about a steward who is caught in the middle of his own ledger, facing the sudden, terrifying end of his career. He is told, 'Prepare a full account of your stewardship, because you can no longer be my steward.'

I want you to hold onto this image: the ledger. It is the image of the accounting we do in our own lives, especially when we are grieving. We look back at the years we had with Benjamin, and we find ourselves trying to balance the books of our own hearts. We wonder if we did enough, if we were enough, if the love we gave was sufficient. We look for the receipts of our devotion, and in the silence of the house, we sometimes fear that the balance is off.

Let us tell the truth of the heart before we look for the comfort. Alan, Thao, Ryan, and all of you who hold the memory of Benjamin Vo as a sacred trust: it has been four months. We know the reality of the empty space at the table. We know that the house, which once hummed with the sound of a brilliant boy coding his games, talking about the mechanics of a Boeing 737, or sharing a laugh about his 'con chim airlines,' now feels like a place where the air is thinner. You are carrying a cross that is not a metaphor; it is a weight of bone and blood and memory. You are allowed to be tired. You are allowed to feel the ache of the missing. You are allowed to be human, and you are allowed to be broken. 

There is a temptation, when we carry this kind of sorrow, to look back at the path we walked and wonder if we missed a sign. We wonder if we could have seen something earlier, or done something differently, or if we failed in some hidden way. Let us lift that stone from your hearts right now. You missed nothing. You were the parents and the brother that Benjamin was given. You loved him with a completeness that filled his fifteen years with the richness of the world. You walked the globe with him, you shared the meals, you witnessed the brilliance of his mind and the gentleness of his spirit. God does not accuse you, and you must not accuse yourselves. Some sorrows in this fragile world arrive entirely beyond human reach, untouched by anything anyone did or failed to do. You are not to blame. Let that heavy stone fall to the ground; you are absolved. You were faithful. You were present. You were love in action. Do not let the enemy of your peace convince you that there is a missing entry in your ledger of love. You gave everything. And in the eyes of God, that is enough.

Now, let the Gospel break in. The steward in the story is in a panic. He is not strong enough to dig, and he is ashamed to beg. He is facing the end of his world, and he doesn't know how to survive it. So, he does something radical. He calls in his master’s debtors and he slashes their debts. He changes the ledger. He realizes that the only way to survive is to stop hoarding and start giving. He realizes that his security is not in what he keeps, but in how he cares for others. Jesus commends him not for his dishonesty, but for his prudence—for realizing that the only thing that matters when the world is ending is the mercy we show to others. 

Benjamin understood this. Think of that moment you shared with us: when he offered his entire piggy bank to help his uncle William. He didn't need to break it, he didn't need to count it out, he didn't need to empty it. The offer itself was the truth of his soul. He had already learned the secret of the kingdom: that we are not here to balance our ledgers; we are here to pour out our lives. He was a boy who knew that the true currency of heaven is not gold, but the kindness we show to those who are suffering. That is the boy you raised. That is the boy who is now at the banquet of heaven, interceding for you. He is not a memory; he is a living soul, fully alive in the love of God. He is a guest who has already taken his seat, and he is waiting for the rest of his family to arrive. 

Ryan, you are a brother who carries a unique, holy weight. You know the memories better than anyone. You know the games you coded, the dreams you shared, the simple, everyday life of being brothers. You are not just a brother who remains; you are a brother who continues the story. When you look at the sky, when you think of the future, remember that you are not doing it alone. You are carrying the legacy of his joy. You are a witness to the world that love is not a finite resource. It is a well that never runs dry. Keep being the boy who reaches out. Keep being the one who values the small, human moments. You are a vital part of this family of four, and your life is a testament to the fact that love is the most durable thing we possess. Your brother's love is not gone; it is woven into the very fabric of who you are becoming.

We hear in the letter to the Philippians today: 'But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we also await a savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. He will change our lowly body to conform with his glorified Body.' This is the turn of the heart. Paul is telling us that the ledger of this world—the one that measures our success by our careers, our health, or our longevity—is not the real ledger. Our true citizenship is not here. We are pilgrims. We are waiting for the One who will take our broken, weary, grieving bodies and change them into something glorious. We are waiting for the One who will take the empty chair, the missing voice, and the ache of the last four months, and transform them into a reunion that will never end. 

Think of the dream you had, Alan. You were waiting in line to buy ice cream, and Ben paid. That is the image of the kingdom. It is the image of the one who has gone before us, the one who is now in the position of the steward of grace, waiting to welcome you. He is not distant. He is not gone. He is simply ahead, preparing the way. He is the one who will one day stand at the door of the Father’s house and say, 'I am here, and my family is with me.' That dream was a whisper from heaven. It was a reminder that the bond you share is not broken by death. It is only changed, deepened, and held in the eternal keeping of God.

There is a peace that comes from knowing that we are held. It is not a peace that takes away the pain, but it is a peace that keeps us from being destroyed by it. It is the peace of knowing that Benjamin is waiting. He is waiting in the light, he is waiting in the place where there is no more struggling, no more darkness, only the clear, bright presence of the Father. He is waiting for you with that same sweet, gentle smile that you remember so vividly. That smile is the sign that the work is going well. That smile is the promise that the reunion is certain. He is a light in the world, and he is shining for you. He is the one who has already passed the test, as he said in your dream: 'Ba ơi, test nào con cũng qua hết.' He is home. And because he is home, you are never truly lost. 

So, what do you carry out the door today? Not a summary, not a heavy burden, but one small, doable thing: when the grief rises and the house feels too quiet, pause. Close your eyes. Imagine the Lord reaching into the silence, and imagine Benjamin smiling at you from the other side. Let yourself be gathered. Trust that you are held. And walk out into the world with the quiet, unshakeable hope that the love you share is the most powerful force in the universe. It is stronger than death. It is more enduring than time. And it is the very thing that will bring you home to each other. You are not a broken family. You are a family of four, and you are being held in the palm of God's hand. Keep your heart open to that truth. Keep your eyes on the light. And remember that he is watching over you, always, with love that knows no end. Amen.
spiritual_communion: My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love You above all things, and I desire to receive You into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive You sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace You as if You were already there and unite myself wholly to You. Never permit me to be separated from You. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you and keep you, may He let His face shine upon you and be gracious to you, and may He give you His peace. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
petition_call: In our need, we turn to the Lord and say:
standing_petitions: For our beloved Benjamin, and for all who have gone before us marked with the sign of faith, that they may rest in the eternal light and peace of Christ, we pray to the Lord.
For all who are grieving, especially Ben’s parents and his brother Ryan, that they may be consoled by the promise of the Resurrection and find strength in the love of God, we pray to the Lord.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
Join with others in being imitators of me, brothers and sisters, 
and observe those who thus conduct themselves 
according to the model you have in us.
For many, as I have often told you 
and now tell you even in tears, 
conduct themselves as enemies of the cross of Christ.
Their end is destruction.
Their God is their stomach; 
their glory is in their “shame.”
Their minds are occupied with earthly things.
But our citizenship is in heaven, 
and from it we also await a savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.
He will change our lowly body
to conform with his glorified Body 
by the power that enables him also 
to bring all things into subjection to himself.Therefore, my brothers and sisters,
whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, 
in this way stand firm in the Lord, beloved.

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R. (1) Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord.
I rejoiced because they said to me,
“We will go up to the house of the LORD.”
And now we have set foot
within your gates, O Jerusalem.
R. Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord.
Jerusalem, built as a city
with compact unity.
To it the tribes go up,
the tribes of the LORD.
R. Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord.
According to the decree for Israel,
to give thanks to the name of the LORD.
In it are set up judgment seats,
seats for the house of David.
R. Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
Jesus said to his disciples, “A rich man had a steward
who was reported to him for squandering his property.
He summoned him and said,
‘What is this I hear about you?
Prepare a full account of your stewardship,
because you can no longer be my steward.’
The steward said to himself, ‘What shall I do,
now that my master is taking the position of steward away from me?
I am not strong enough to dig and I am ashamed to beg.
I know what I shall do so that,
when I am removed from the stewardship,
they may welcome me into their homes.’
He called in his master’s debtors one by one.
To the first he said, ‘How much do you owe my master?’
He replied, ‘One hundred measures of olive oil.’
He said to him, ‘Here is your promissory note.
Sit down and quickly write one for fifty.’
Then to another he said, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’
He replied, ‘One hundred measures of wheat.’  
He said to him, ‘Here is your promissory note;
write one for eighty.’
And the master commended that dishonest steward for acting prudently.
For the children of this world
are more prudent in dealing with their own generation
than the children of light.”
